Lesson 1: Introduction to the piano!
The piano consists of white and black keys!
The black keys are in sets of twos and threes, as shown on the piano.
This pattern of black keys repeats as you go up and down the piano. Use the − and + buttons above the piano to move to lower or higher octaves.
Similarly, a set of eight white keys repeats.
These sets of eight keys are called octaves.
The white keys are named after the first seven letters of the alphabet, namely A, B, C, D, E, F, G.
C is to the left of the two black keys.
The white key to the right of C is D.
The white key after D is E.
The white key after E is F.
The white key after F is G.
The white key after G is A.
The white key after A is B.
The white key after B is C! And so it repeats.
The keys towards the right of the piano sound higher.
The keys towards the left of the piano sound lower.
Accidentals and names of the black notes:
From one key to the nearest key is called a semitone.
The semitone to the right of a key is described by a sharp (♯).
A sharp raises a key/note one semitone higher.
The semitone to the left of a key is called a flat (♭).
A flat (♭) lowers a note/key by one semitone.
The white keys are called naturals (♮).
Names of the black keys:
The black keys are named relative to the white keys a semitone away from them.
The black key a semitone to the right of C is called C sharp (C♯).
It is also called D flat (D♭) because it is a semitone to the left of D.
The black key before E is called E flat (E♭) because it is a semitone to the left of E.
The rest of the black keys are named in a similar fashion, relative to the white keys a semitone away from them.
The C major scale on the piano keyboard
Sitting and hand position:
Sit upright at the middle of the piano and keep your fingers slightly curved.
Correct sitting posture and curved finger position
Lesson 2: Fingerings and rudiments of music
Finger numbers for both hands: thumbs are 1, little fingers are 5
The C five-finger position
Play the following keys with the correct fingerings.
Right hand: play C, D, E, F, G with fingers 1 to 5
Now play with the left hand (LH). The keyboard moves down to C3 for you.
Left hand: play C, D, E, F, G with fingers 5 to 1
Rudiments: musical sounds are written using characters called notes.
These notes are named after the first seven letters of the alphabet, namely A, B, C, D, E, F, G.
The notes are placed on what is called a staff or stave.
The staff consists of five lines and four spaces.
An empty staff with five lines and four spaces
These lines and spaces are counted from bottom to top.
The names of the lines and spaces of the staff are determined by what is termed a clef.
There are two clefs required for the piano.
1. The Treble or G clef
A staff with a treble clef
2. The Bass or F clef
A staff with a bass clef
The Treble or G clef is drawn from the second line of the staff. The second line is thus named G.
The names of the treble staff
Treble staff with the names of each line and space
These acronyms can help you remember the names of the treble notes.
Lines: Every Good Boy Does Fine
Spaces: F A C E
Ledger lines:
These are short horizontal lines added to extend the staff.
Notes written on ledger lines above and below the staff
The first ledger line below the treble staff is known as middle C.
Middle C is the C in the middle of the piano. It divides the piano into two halves.
The treble staff is usually played with the right hand.
Play the following notes on the piano. Remember to use the correct fingerings.
C D E, C D E, I can play
C D E, E D C, E D C
Up and down to middle C
Now play the C major scale using the correct fingerings.
C major scale with fingerings
And lastly, try this tune in 4/4 time.
A short tune on the treble staff in 4/4 time
Lesson 3: The bass staff
The bass clef is drawn from the fourth line of the staff. That line is called F.
Bass staff with the names of each line and space
The names of the bass staff can be remembered with the following acronyms.
Lines: Good Boys Deserve Fudge Always
Spaces: All Cows Eat Grass
The bass notes are usually played with the left hand.
Now play the following with the left hand, remembering to use the correct fingerings. The keyboard moves down to C3 for you.
Left hand five-finger scale: C D E F G with fingers 5 4 3 2 1
Left hand exercise, part 1
Left hand exercise, part 2
The grand staff:
The grand staff is made of the treble and bass staves joined by a brace.

Lesson 4: Notes
Note values and their names
Note values and their beats
The note tree: how note values divide
Bar lines: these are vertical lines that cut through the staff. They divide the staff into equal measures of time.
Bar lines dividing the staff into measures
Time signatures:
Common time signatures
A time signature of 4/4 means there are four quarter notes (crotchets) in a bar. The crotchet gets one beat.
A tune in 4/4 time
Similarly, a time signature of 3/4 means there are three quarter notes (crotchets) in a bar. The crotchet gets one beat.
A time signature of 6/8 means there are six eighth notes (quavers) in a bar. The quaver gets one beat.
